title: Adam Sandler's Eight Crazy Nights
full_review:
The cartoon feature "Adam Sandler's Eight Crazy Nights" (Columbia) cloaks itself as a tale of redemption that unfolds during Hanukkah and the days leading up to Christmas.

Despite multiple references to the parallel holy seasons and to the good that can be achieved through selfless behavior, the feature-length cartoon dwells on abundant rudeness and gross behavior that are designed to delight an irreverent, impressionable young audience.

The depiction of Hanukkah and the anticipation of Christmas are entirely secular, although the central character does finally perform good deeds, which coincide with, more than they're directly linked to, the season at hand.

Adam Sandler, who is credited with creating the derivative story, gives voice to all three of the principal characters -- Davey Stone, Whitey Duvall and Eleanore Duvall -- as well as to a deer.

Davey Stone is a 33-year-old Jewish wastrel and Sandler look-alike, a once-promising boy who began acting miserably toward everyone else when his parents were killed in an auto accident.

Whitey, a fireplug-sized elderly referee of boys' basketball with an annoyingly high voice, takes Davey under wing and even provides him with shelter.

Whitey's twin sister Eleanore, whose wigs and thick glasses are nearly as large as she, is less trusting about the arrangement. But because the film unfolds from the vantage of a young person, Eleanore is depicted as being exceptionally out of it.

Directed by Seth Kearsley, the picture gives Davey and others about an hour to heap ridicule onto people less hip and cynical than themselves including the Duvalls and a boy mortified by his enlarged breasts.

Davey's inevitable redemption, ever so loosely linked to the passing of the Jewish holidays, isn't just unpersuasive. It becomes a license to let him behave as outrageously as he can beforehand.

"Eight Crazy Nights" is packed with behavior ranging from the rude (long burps, public drunkenness, cruel remarks, flipping the bird) to bad taste involving epilepsy and features many instances of gross-out behavior involving assorted bodily functions and degrading physical abuse.

Not the least of its cliches is Davey's renewed interest in a single mother (Jackie Titone voicing the part of Jennifer) and in her son Benjamin (Austin Stout).

Some moderately appealing songs are saddled with crude lyrics.

Perhaps more offensive is the abundance of shopping mall product placement, sometimes accompanied by dialogue laced with advertising.

Audiences in search of seasonal sentiments won't want to wade through the movie's first hour. Sandler's core audience is just as likely to find the concluding scenes too sappy for what leads up to them.

Because of recurring vulgarity that takes many forms, a lot of it involving body functions and off-putting images, and brief alcohol abuse, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
